Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were American Communist spies who passed atomic bomb secrets to the Soviet Union during the Cold War. Executed by electric chair in nineteen fifty-three, they became martyrs to some and traitors to others, their trial and death a defining moment of anti-Communist hysteria in nineteen-fifties America.

Julius was an electrical engineer at Los Alamos who was recruited by Soviet intelligence and ran a spy ring that transmitted classified nuclear research to Moscow during World War II and after. His wife Ethel typed up handwritten notes from her brother David Greenglass, another spy, detailing uranium enrichment procedures and bomb design, though her exact level of involvement remains contested by historians.

The couple was arrested in nineteen fifty during the FBI's counterintelligence sweep following Klaus Fuchs's exposure. They were convicted under the Espionage Act based on testimony from Greenglass and others. Sentenced to death in April nineteen fifty-one, their execution on June nineteenth, nineteen fifty-three made them the first American civilians executed for espionage, drawing international protest and conspiracy theories that persist today.

Some historians argue that Ethel was largely peripheral to the espionage and was prosecuted partly to pressure Julius into confession. However, declassified Soviet files confirm Julius's guilt but have done little to resolve Ethel's role in the conspiracy.
